{{Short description|Concept in three-dimensional geometry}}
In [[geometry]], '''tetrahedron packing''' is the problem of arranging identical regular [[tetrahedron|tetrahedra]] throughout three-dimensional space so as to fill the maximum possible fraction of space. 

[[File:Tetrahedron packing structure png.png|thumb|The currently densest known packing structure for regular tetrahedra is a [[double lattice]] of [[triangular bipyramid]]s and fills 85.63% of space]]

Currently, the best lower bound achieved on the optimal [[packing density|packing fraction]] of regular tetrahedra is 85.63%.<ref name="chen2010">
{{cite journal
 | first1 = Elizabeth R. | last1 = Chen
 | first2 = Michael | last2 = Engel
 | first3 = Sharon C. | last3 = Glotzer
 | title = Dense crystalline dimer packings of regular tetrahedra
 | year = 2010
 | volume = 44
 | number = 2
 | pages = 253–280
 | doi = 10.1007/s00454-010-9273-0
 | journal = [[Discrete & Computational Geometry]]
| arxiv = 1001.0586| s2cid = 18523116
 }}</ref> Tetrahedra do not [[tessellation|tile]] space,<ref>{{cite journal|first=D. J.|last=Struik|author-link=Dirk Jan Struik|title= Het probleem 'De Impletione Loci'|year=1925|journal=[[Nieuw Archief voor Wiskunde]]|series=2nd ser|jfm=52.0002.04|volume=15|pages=121–134}}</ref> and an upper bound below 100% (namely, 1 − (2.6...)·10<sup>−25</sup>) has been reported.<ref>{{cite journal|author1=Simon Gravel|author2=Veit Elser|author3=Yoav Kallus|doi=10.1007/s00454-010-9304-x|title=Upper bound on the packing density of regular tetrahedra and octahedra|year=2010|journal=[[Discrete & Computational Geometry]]|arxiv=1008.2830|volume=46|issue=4|pages=799–818|s2cid=18908213}}</ref>

==Historical results==

[[File:Tetrahedral Milk Carton Arrangement.jpg|thumb|right|Tetrahedral packaging]]

[[Aristotle]] claimed that tetrahedra could fill space completely.<ref>{{cite news|title=Mysteries in Packing Regular Tetrahedra|url=http://www.ams.org/notices/201211/rtx121101540p.pdf|date=2012-12-04|author=[[Jeffrey Lagarias]] and Chuanming Zong}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Jeffrey Lagarias and Chuanming Zong to receive 2015 Conant Prize|url=https://www.eurekalert.org/pub_releases/2014-12/ams-jla120314.php|date=2014-12-03|author=News Release}}</ref>
 
In 2006, [[John Horton Conway|Conway]] and Torquato showed that a packing fraction about 72% can be obtained by constructing a non-Bravais lattice packing of tetrahedra (with multiple particles with generally different orientations per repeating unit), and thus they showed that the best tetrahedron packing cannot be a lattice packing (with one particle per repeating unit such that each particle has a common orientation).<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Conway | first1=J. H. | title=Packing, tiling, and covering with tetrahedra | journal=[[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences]] | volume=103 | issue=28 | pages=10612–10617 | year=2006 | doi=10.1073/pnas.0601389103 | pmid=16818891 | pmc=1502280 | bibcode=2006PNAS..10310612C| doi-access=free }}</ref> These packing constructions almost doubled the optimal Bravais-lattice-packing fraction 36.73% obtained by Hoylman.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Hoylman | first1=Douglas J. | title=The densest lattice packing of tetrahedra | journal=[[Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society]] | volume=76 | pages=135–138 | year=1970 | doi=10.1090/S0002-9904-1970-12400-4| doi-access=free | hdl=10150/288016 | hdl-access=free }}</ref> In 2007 and 2010, Chaikin and coworkers experimentally showed that tetrahedron-like dice can randomly pack in a finite container up to a packing fraction between 75% and 76%.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Jaoshvili | first1=Alexander | last2=Esakia | first2=Andria | last3=Porrati | first3=Massimo | last4=Chaikin | first4=Paul M. | title=Experiments on the Random Packing of Tetrahedral Dice | journal=[[Physical Review Letters]] | volume=104 | issue=18 | year=2010 | doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.104.185501 | pmid=20482187 | bibcode=2010PhRvL.104r5501J | article-number=185501| url=https://zenodo.org/record/895669 | hdl=10919/24495 | hdl-access=free }}</ref> In 2008, Chen was the first to propose a packing of hard, regular tetrahedra that packed more densely than spheres, demonstrating numerically a packing fraction of 77.86%.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Chen | first1=Elizabeth R. | title=A Dense Packing of Regular Tetrahedra | journal=[[Discrete & Computational Geometry]] | volume=40 | issue=2 | pages=214–240 | year=2008 | doi=10.1007/s00454-008-9101-y| arxiv=0908.1884 | s2cid=32166668 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1=Cohn | first1=Henry | title=Mathematical physics: A tight squeeze |journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]] | volume=460 | issue=7257 | pages=801–802 | year=2009 | pmid=19675632 | doi=10.1038/460801a | bibcode=2009Natur.460..801C| s2cid=5157975 }}</ref> A further improvement was made in 2009 by Torquato and Jiao, who compressed Chen's structure using a computer algorithm to a packing fraction of 78.2021%.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Torquato | first1=S. | last2=Jiao | first2=Y. | title=Dense packings of the Platonic and Archimedean solids |journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]] | volume=460 | issue=7257 | pages=876–879 | year=2009 | pmid=19675649 | doi=10.1038/nature08239 | bibcode=2009Natur.460..876T|arxiv = 0908.4107 | s2cid=52819935 }}</ref>

In mid-2009 Haji-Akbari et al. showed, using [[Monte Carlo method|MC]] simulations of initially random systems that at packing densities &gt;50% an equilibrium fluid of hard tetrahedra spontaneously transforms to a dodecagonal [[quasicrystal]], which can be compressed to 83.24%. They also reported a glassy, disordered packing at densities exceeding 78%. For a periodic approximant to a quasicrystal with an 82-tetrahedron unit cell, they obtained a packing density as high as 85.03%.<ref name="Haji-Akbari2009">{{cite journal | last1=Haji-Akbari | first1=Amir | last2=Engel | first2=Michael | last3=Keys | first3=Aaron S. | last4=Zheng | first4=Xiaoyu | last5=Petschek | first5=Rolfe G. | last6=Palffy-Muhoray | first6=Peter | last7=Glotzer | first7=Sharon C. | title=Disordered, quasicrystalline and crystalline phases of densely packed tetrahedra |journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]] | volume=462 | issue=7274 | pages=773–777 | year=2009 | pmid=20010683 | doi=10.1038/nature08641 | bibcode=2009Natur.462..773H|arxiv = 1012.5138 | s2cid=4412674 }}</ref>

In late 2009, a new, much simpler family of packings with a packing fraction of 85.47% was discovered by Kallus, Elser, and Gravel.<ref>{{Cite journal
 | first1 = Yoav | last1 = Kallus
 | first2 = Veit | last2 = Elser
 | first3 = Simon | last3 = Gravel
 | year = 2010
 | title = Dense Periodic Packings of Tetrahedra with Small Repeating Units
 | journal = [[Discrete & Computational Geometry]]
 | volume = 44| issue = 2| pages = 245–252
 | doi = 10.1007/s00454-010-9254-3
 | arxiv=0910.5226
| s2cid = 13385357
 }}</ref> These packings were also the basis of a slightly improved packing obtained by Torquato and Jiao at the end of 2009 with a packing fraction of 85.55%,<ref>
{{Cite arXiv
 | first1 = S. | last1 = Torquato
 | first2 = Y. | last2 = Jiao
 | year = 2009
 | title = Analytical Constructions of a Family of Dense Tetrahedron Packings and the Role of Symmetry
 | eprint = 0912.4210
 | class =cond-mat.stat-mech 
}}</ref> and by Chen, Engel, and Glotzer in early 2010 with a packing fraction of 85.63%.<ref name="chen2010"/>  The Chen, Engel and Glotzer result currently stands as the densest known packing of hard, regular tetrahedra. The quasicrystal approximant structure<ref name="Haji-Akbari2009"/> packs denser than this [[double lattice]] of [[triangular bipyramid]]s when tetrahedra are slightly rounded (the [[Minkowski sum]] of a tetrahedron and a sphere), making the 82-tetrahedron crystal the largest unit cell for a densest packing of identical particles to date.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Jin |first1=Weiwei |last2=Lu |first2=Peng |last3=Li |first3=Shuixiang |title=Evolution of the dense packings of spherotetrahedral particles: from ideal tetrahedra to spheres |journal=Scientific Reports |date=December 2015 |volume=5 |issue=1 |article-number=15640 |doi=10.1038/srep15640|pmid=26490670 |pmc=4614866 |bibcode=2015NatSR...515640J |doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Relationship to other packing problems==
Because the earliest lower bound known for packings of tetrahedra was less than that of [[sphere packing|spheres]], it was suggested that the regular tetrahedra might be a counterexample to [[Ulam's packing conjecture|Ulam's conjecture]] that the optimal density for [[sphere packing|packing congruent spheres]] is smaller than that for any other convex body.  However, the more recent results have shown that this is not the case.
